title: Calendar Girls
full_review:
Calendar Girls (Touchstone) is an enjoyable but mostly forgettable British comedy in which prim-and-proper English matrons pose naked for a calendar to raise money for charity.
The film's appeal lies in the few laughs it manages and a likable cast. Yet its flimsy premise doesn't have the energy to sustain the entire film and the third act just peters out. It's as if screenwriters Juliette Towhidi and Tim Firth didn't quite know how to wrap things up so they slapped something together that they hoped would pass.

However, "Calendar Girls" is given a boost by top-notch performances from Helen Mirren and Julie Walters. Their charming characters, Chris (Mirren) and Annie (Walters) are best friends who see each other through thick and thin. Together they endure tedious lectures on such riveting subjects as broccoli, milk marketing and rugs at the Women's Institute, a gathering of Yorkshire women who meet for "enlightenment, fun and friendship." Sitting in the back of the lecture room, they try to contain their peals of laughter as the latest speaker drones on about a family vacation.

As he did in the 2000 film "Saving Grace," director Nigel Cole once again places proper English people in socially touchy situations, throwing the typical stuffed-shirt impression of Brits out the window. After Annie's husband dies of leukemia, Chris tries to help her grieving friend feel useful again. She comes up with this zany idea to raise money for the local hospital by having their middle-aged friends at the Women's Institute pose naked -- or, as she pitches it more delicately, "nude" -- for a calendar. The women would be in familiar poses -- making jam, watering flowers, knitting afghans -- with props strategically placed so that, although their skin is exposed, their very private parts would be concealed.

Cole handles the nudity in a mostly modest way, showing skin -- a bare thigh here, shoulders and arms there -- rather than actual female anatomy. The nudity is suggested rather than stated.
Predictably, the calendar is a wild success, which, just as predictably, causes tension between Annie and Chris as the calendar girls are pressed for interviews, photo-ops and even a jaunt across the Atlantic for a spot on Jay Leno's "Tonight Show."

Chris' teenage son, who is beginning to explore his own sexuality, is unnerved by his mother's sudden stardom, especially the reason behind it. But even when he gets busted for smoking marijuana (although it turns out to be oregano), Chris pushes full steam ahead, ignoring problems at home for the limelight. This time she's the one that needs Annie to pull her back to Earth and remind her of what's really important.

The subtext of the film (which was inspired by a true story) is that in this youth-centered world, older women can have plenty of sex appeal. The film's cast of veteran actors proves this. The film also succeeds by gently mixing humor within the context of real-life situations, such as the death of a spouse, ornery teens acting out and husbands feeling a bit resentful and left out.

All in all, "Calendar Girls" is amusing despite its flaws.

Because of a flash of nudity with several scenes suggestive of nudity, a few instances of crass language and brief drug content, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
